claims.source: PPL1-γ1pedc was labeled with these FISH probes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), confirming expression of NOS1 or NOS4 in these cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: In the MB lobes, the γ1pedc and γ5 compartments showed enriched anti-NOS immunoreactivity.
claims.source: In the MB lobes, the γ1pedc and γ5 compartments showed enriched anti-NOS immunoreactivity, as expected from the RNA-Seq data (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: NOS colocalizes with γ1pedc's terminals.
claims.source: Furthermore, we confirmed colocalization of NOS with γ1pedc's terminals by expansion microscopy and lattice light sheet microscopy (ExM LLSM; Figure 3F and G, Video 1) (Chen et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2019; Tillberg et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ExM LLSM data shown in Figure 3F and G, Video 1.

claims.claim: Feeding flies the competitive NOS inhibitor L-NNA reduced valence-inverted memory formation in a dose-dependent manner.
claims.source: We found that this treatment reduced valence-inverted memory formation in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: When dopamine levels were restored by feeding L-DOPA and carbidopa, L-NNA fed flies showed a normal level of negative-valence odor memory formation in response to pairing an odor with PPL1-γ1pedc activation.
claims.source: First, when we bypassed the TH mutant by feeding L-DOPA and carbidopa to restore dopamine levels, the L-NNA fed flies showed a normal level of negative-valence odor memory formation in response to pairing an odor with PPL1- γ1pedc activation (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The effect of L-NNA feeding was cell-type specific; memory formed by activation of either PPL1-γ1pedc or PAM-γ5/β'2a was affected but that formed by activation of PPL1-γ2α'1, was not.
claims.source: Second, the effect of L-NNA feeding was cell-type specific; memory formed by activation of either PPL1-γ1pedc or PAM-γ5/β'2a was affected but that formed by activation of PPL1-γ2α'1, was not (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Expressing NOS-RNAi in all PPL1 DANs resulted in negative-valence memory in the TH mutant background.
claims.source: We obtained consistent results in knockdown experiments where we expressed NOS-RNAi in all PPL1 DANs (Figure 4C). In this case, the negative-valence memory observed with NOS-RNAi in the TH mutant background is consistent with the presence of a different cotransmitter in PPL1-γ2α'1 (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: When NOS was ectopically expressed in PPL1-α3, the same training protocol induced a positive-valence memory in TH mutant flies.
claims.source: TH mutant flies formed no odor association with PPL1-α3 activation, but when NOS was ectopically expressed in the α3 compartment, the same training protocol induced a positive-valence memory (Figure 4D and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claims.claim: Ectopic expression of NOS in PPL1-γ2α'1 resulted in valence inversion phenotype.
claims.source: Similarly, ectopic expression of NOS in PPL1-γ2α'1 also resulted in valence inversion phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: NO was able to form an association of opposite valence to that formed by dopamine.
claims.source: In other words, NO was able to form an association of opposite valence to that formed by dopamine.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference from the ectopic expression experiments shown in Figure 4D, E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: RNA-seq data revealed expression of the subunits of soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC), Gycα99B and Gycβ100B, in KCs, DANs, and MBONs.
claims.source: RNA-seq data revealed expression of the subunits of soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC), Gycα99B and Gycβ100B, in KCs, DANs, and MBONs (Figure 5A–B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A–B.

claims.claim: Drosophila sGC is activated upon binding NO.
claims.source: Similar to its mammalian homologs, Drosophila sGC is activated upon binding NO (Morton et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Morton et al., 2005.

claims.claim: A protein trap Gycβ100B-EGFP fusion protein was broadly expressed in the MB lobes.
claims.source: Consistent with these transcriptomic data, we observed that a protein trap Gycβ100B-EGFP fusion protein (MI08892; Venken et al., 2011) was broadly expressed in the MB lobes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Venken et al., 2011.

claims.claim: RNAi knockdown of Gycβ100B in KCs abolished the valence-inverted memory induced by activation of PPL1-γ1pedc in a TH mutant background.
claims.source: We found that a reduction in Gycβ100B produced in this way abolished the valence-inverted memory induced by activation of PPL1-γ1pedc in a TH mutant background (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Flies carrying MB-switch driven Gycβ100B-RNAi do not have a general defect in learning.
claims.source: Although MB-switch showed significant leaky expression without RU-486 feeding under our experimental conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F), we could restore normal aversive memory by feeding TH mutant flies L-DOPA (Figure 5C), indicating that flies carrying MB-switch driven Gycβ100B-RNAi do not have a general defect in learning.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F.

claims.claim: NO functions as cotransmitter that is released by DANs and acts on sGC in postsynaptic KCs to regulate cGMP levels.
claims.source: Taken together, our data argue strongly that NO functions as cotransmitter that is released by DANs and acts on sGC in postsynaptic KCs to regulate cGMP levels, although our results do not exclude the possibility that NO has other targets.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference from the data presented in Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claims.claim: Optogenetic stimulation of PPL1-γ1pedc in a TH-mutant background can induce a prolonged increase in calcium levels in MBON-γ1pedc>α/β, which was suppressed by L-NNA.
claims.source: Indeed, both MBONs and DANs express sGC (Figure 5B) and we found that optogenetic stimulation of PPL1-γ1pedc in a TH-mutant background can induce a prolonged increase in calcium levels in MBON-γ1pedc>α/β, which was suppressed by L-NNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: DANs expressing sGC in other compartments did not respond to stimulation of PPL1-γ1pedc in a TH-mutant background.
claims.source: However, DANs expressing sGC in other compartments did not respond to stimulation of PPL1-γ1pedc in a TH-mutant background (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), raising the possibility that NO may not be able to diffuse over the 30 µm distances required to reach those compartments.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: PPL1-γ1pedc induces a valence inverted memory when its activity precedes an odor such that the odor predicts relief from punishment.
claims.source: PPL1-γ1pedc induces a valence inverted memory when its activity precedes an odor such that the odor predicts relief from punishment (Aso and Rubin, 2016; Tanimoto et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aso and Rubin, 2016; Tanimoto et al., 2004.

claims.claim: NOS is dispensable for timing dependent inversion of memory valence.
claims.source: NOS is dispensable for this timing dependent inversion of memory valence (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), an observation consistent with a recent report that timing dependent inversion of long-term-depression of KC-to-MBON synapses to long-term-potentiation is mediated by different dopamine receptors (Handler et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and a citation to Handler et al., 2019.

claims.claim: RNAi knockdown of scrib impaired NO-dependent memory in TH-mutant flies.
claims.source: RNAi knockdown of scrib impaired NO-dependent memory in TH-mutant flies (Figure 5D), suggesting a role of NO in regulating memory stability.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: In wild-type flies, PPL1-γ1pedc activation as brief as 10 s can induce significant negative-valence memory.
claims.source: In wild-type flies, PPL1-γ1pedc activation as brief as 10 s can induce significant negative-valence memory.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Blocking NOS activity with L-NNA did not affect the memory scores observed shortly after a wide range of training protocols.
claims.source: Blocking NOS activity with L-NNA did not affect the memory scores observed shortly after a wide range of training protocols (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Longer and repetitive training was required to induce robust NO-dependent positive-valence memory in the absence of dopamine.
claims.source: In contrast, longer and repetitive training was required to induce robust NO-dependent positive-valence memory in the absence of dopamine (Figure 6A–B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A–B.

claims.claim: NO-dependent memory develops slowly over time.
claims.source: When we used a single cycle of training, we found that NO-dependent memory develops slowly over time. Memory scores were not significantly different from zero at 1, 3, 5 min after training, and only became significant after 10 min.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: NO-dependent memories were long lasting and were still more than half maximal after 6 hr.
claims.source: Once formed, however, these NO-dependent memories were long lasting and were still more than half maximal after 6 hr (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Expression of NOS-RNAi or L-NNA feeding prolonged the retention of memories induced by either optogenetic training with PPL1-γ1pedc or odor-shock conditioning.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that expression of NOS-RNAi or L-NNA feeding prolonged the retention of memories induced by either optogenetic training with PPL1-γ1pedc or odor-shock conditioning (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B.

claims.claim: PPL1-γ1pedc fails to induce long-lasting memory even after 10x repetitive training at spaced intervals.
claims.source: However, PPL1-γ1pedc fails to induce long-lasting memory even after 10x repetitive training at spaced intervals (Aso and Rubin, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Aso and Rubin, 2016.

claims.claim: Other DANs from the PPL1 cluster that do not exhibit significant NOS expression, PPL1-α3 or a combination of PPL1-γ2α'1 and PPL1-α'2α2, are able to induce stable memory lasting for 4 days after 10x spaced training.
claims.source: In contrast, other DANs from the PPL1 cluster that do not exhibit significant NOS expression, PPL1-α3 or a combination of PPL1-γ2α'1 and PPL1-α'2α2, are able to induce stable memory lasting for 4 days after 10x spaced training (Aso and Rubin, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Aso and Rubin, 2016.

claims.claim: Spaced training with PPL1-γ1pedc induced memory lasting 1 day when NOS signaling was compromised, either by knockdown with RNAi or inhibition by L-NNA.
claims.source: Spaced training with PPL1-γ1pedc induced memory lasting 1 day when NOS signaling was compromised, either by knockdown with RNAi (Figure 6E) or inhibition by L-NNA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The valence-inverted memories formed in the γ1pedc compartment following repetitive training in TH mutants lasted 1 day after training.
claims.source: The valence-inverted memories formed in the γ1pedc compartment following repetitive training in TH mutants also lasted 1 day after training (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: In wild-type flies, odor preference can be altered by a single trial of reversal conditioning with PPL1-γ1pedc activation.
claims.source: In wild-type flies, odor preference can be altered by a single trial of reversal conditioning with PPL1-γ1pedc activation (Figure 7B, left)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B, left.

claims.claim: When NOS was inhibited, switching odor preference required a repetition of reversal conditioning.
claims.source: whereas this process became slower and required more training when NOS was inhibited (Figure 7B; center), such that switching odor preference required a repetition of reversal conditioning.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B; center.

claims.claim: In TH mutants, NO-dependent memory was altered by reversal conditioning, but with an even slower time course.
claims.source: In TH mutants, NO-dependent memory was also altered by reversal conditioning, but with an even slower time course (Figure 7B; right).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B; right.

claims.claim: Exposure to odors alone did not change the existing memory.
claims.source: The second type of new experience, exposure to odors alone, did not change the existing memory in this assay (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: DAN activation alone quickly reduced conditioned odor response in wild-type flies.
claims.source: The third type of new experience, DAN activation alone, quickly reduced conditioned odor response in wild-type flies.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Inhibiting NOS slowed the reduction of conditioned odor response by DAN activation alone.
claims.source: Inhibiting NOS slowed this process (Figure 7D; center).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D; center.

claims.claim: NO-dependent memory was reduced by unpaired activation of DANs, but it took five trials to detect significant reduction.
claims.source: NO-dependent memory was also reduced by unpaired activation of DANs, but it took five trials to detect significant reduction (Figure 7D; right).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D; right.

claims.claim: Both the slow formation and the persistence of NO-dependent memory facilitate the fast updating of memories stored in NOS-positive MB compartments in response to changing conditions.
claims.source: These results suggest that both the slow formation and the persistence of NO-dependent memory facilitate the fast updating of memories stored in NOS-positive MB compartments in response to changing conditions.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference from the data presented in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The multiplicative model provides a good match to the behavioral data.
claims.source: We found that the multiplicative model provides a good match to our data (Figure 8C, blue curve).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Assuming that spontaneous activity in DANs leads to memory decay accounted for the NO-dependent reduction in memory lifetime.
claims.source: Assuming that spontaneous activity in DANs leads to memory decay (Plaçais et al., 2012; Berry et al., 2018; Sitaraman et al., 2015) accounted for the NO-dependent reduction in memory lifetime that we observed (Figure 8E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 8E and citations to Plaçais et al., 2012; Berry et al., 2018; Sitaraman et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The model cannot account for the enhanced persistence of memories after 10x training for DA or NO-null conditions, suggesting a recruitment of additional consolidation mechanisms after spaced conditioning.
claims.source: A notable exception is that this model cannot account for the enhanced persistence of memories after 10x training for DA or NO-null conditions (Figure 6E), suggesting a recruitment of additional consolidation mechanisms after spaced conditioning, as previously proposed (Pagani et al., 2009; Tully et al., 1994; Pai et al., 2013; Scheunemann et al., 2018; Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2013; Miyashita et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2012; Akalal et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference from the modeling results and is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Spaced training with PPL-α3 can induce long-lasting memory but it requires at least 3 hr after training to develop.
claims.source: Also, we found that spaced training with PPL-α3 can induce long-lasting memory but it requires at least 3 hr after training to develop (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: Protein synthesis in MBON-α3 in the first 3 hr time window after odor-shock spaced training is required for LTM formation.
claims.source: This observation is consistent with the report that protein synthesis in MBON-α3 in the first 3 hr time window after odor-shock spaced training is required for LTM formation (Pai et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2017)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pai et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Subsets of dopaminergic neurons co-release glutamate or GABA in rodents.
claims.source: In rodents, subsets of dopaminergic neurons co-release glutamate or GABA (Maher and Westbrook, 2008; Stuber et al., 2010; Sulzer et al., 1998; Tecuapetla et al., 2010; Tritsch et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Single-cell expression profiling reveals expression of diverse neuropeptides in dopaminergic neurons in mice and Drosophila.
claims.source: In mice and Drosophila, single-cell expression profiling reveals expression of diverse neuropeptides in dopaminergic neurons (Croset et al., 2018; Poulin et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Croset et al., 2018; Poulin et al., 2014.

claims.claim: EM connectome studies of the mushroom body in adult and larval Drosophila reveal the co-existence of small-clear-core and large-dense-core synaptic vesicles in individual terminals of dopaminergic neurons.
claims.source: EM connectome studies of the mushroom body in adult and larval Drosophila reveal the co-existence of small-clear-core and large-dense-core synaptic vesicles in individual terminals of dopaminergic neurons (Eichler et al., 2017; Takemura et al., 2017)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eichler et al., 2017; Takemura et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The size of the observed large-dense-core vesicles differs between DAN cell types.
claims.source: moreover, the size of the observed large-dense-core vesicles differs between DAN cell types (Takemura et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Takemura et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Drosophila NOS is regulated by Ca2+/calmodulin.
claims.source: Drosophila NOS is regulated by Ca2+/calmodulin (Regulski and Tully, 1995), as is the neuronal isoform of NOS in the mammalian brain (Abu-Soud and Stuehr, 1993)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Regulski and Tully, 1995; Abu-Soud and Stuehr, 1993.

claims.claim: The localization of the NOS1 protein in the axonal terminals of DANs is consistent with NO serving as a cotransmitter.
claims.source: Furthermore, the localization of the NOS1 protein in the axonal terminals of DANs (Figure 3D) is consistent with NO serving as a cotransmitter.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference from the immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: NO acts as a neurotransmitter in the Drosophila mushroom body, in contrast to a proposed cell-autonomous action of NOS in the ellipsoid body.
claims.source: This role contrasts with the proposed cell-autonomous action of NOS in the ellipsoid body, in which NO appears to target proteins within the NOS-expressing ring neurons themselves, rather than conveying a signal to neighboring cells (Kuntz et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference from the data and is contrasted with a citation to Kuntz et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The concentration of Ca2+ in KC axons represents olfactory information during olfactory learning.
claims.source: During olfactory learning, the concentration of Ca2+ in KC axons represents olfactory information.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila mushroom body.

claims.claim: The coincidence of a Ca2+ rise in spiking KCs and activation of the G-protein-coupled Dop1R1 dopamine receptor increases adenylyl cyclase activity.
claims.source: The coincidence of a Ca2+ rise in spiking KCs and activation of the G-protein-coupled Dop1R1 dopamine receptor increases adenylyl cyclase activity (Abrams et al., 1998; Boto et al., 2014; Byrne et al., 1991; Kim et al., 2007; McGuire et al., 2003; Tomchik and Davis, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The resultant cAMP activates protein kinase A.
claims.source: The resultant cAMP in turn activates protein kinase A (Gervasi et al., 2010; Skoulakis et al., 1993), a signaling cascade that is important for synaptic plasticity and memory formation throughout the animal phyla (e.g. Davis et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gervasi et al., 2010; Skoulakis et al., 1993; Davis et al., 1995.

claims.claim: When DANs are activated without KC activity, molecular pathways involving the Dop1R2 receptor, Rac1 and Scribble facilitate decay of memory.
claims.source: In contrast, when DANs are activated without KC activity, and thus during low intracellular Ca2+ in the KCs, molecular pathways involving the Dop1R2 receptor, Rac1 and Scribble facilitate decay of memory (Berry et al., 2012; Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2007; Shuai et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Berry et al., 2012; Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2007; Shuai et al., 2010.

claims.claim: NO-dependent effect requires scribble in KCs, a gene previously reported as a component of active forgetting.
claims.source: Indeed, NO-dependent effect requires scribble in KCs, a gene previously reported as a component of active forgetting (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D and references to previous work on scribble.

claims.claim: In the vertebrate cerebellum, long-term-depression at parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapses induced by climbing fibers can coexist with long-term-potentiation by NO.
claims.source: In the vertebrate cerebellum, which has many architectural similarities to the MB (Farris, 2011; Marr, 1969; Medina et al., 2002), long-term-depression at parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapses (equivalent to KC-MBON synapses) induced by climbing fibers (equivalent to DANs) can coexist with long-term-potentiation by NO (Bredt et al., 1990; Lev-Ram et al., 2002; Shibuki and Okada, 1991).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The balance between LTD and LTP in the cerebellum was suggested to play an important role in preventing memory saturation and allowing reversal of motor learning.
claims.source: In this case, the unaltered net synaptic weight results from a balance between coexisting LTD and LTP rather than recovery from LTD. This balance was suggested to play an important role in preventing memory saturation in the cerebellum and allowing reversal of motor learning.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference from the cited literature on the cerebellum.

claims.claim: Opposing cotransmitters have been observed widely in both invertebrate and vertebrate neurons.
claims.source: Opposing cotransmitters have been observed widely in both invertebrate and vertebrate neurons (Nusbaum et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nusbaum et al., 2017.

claims.claim: A common feature of opposing cotransmitters is that the transmitters have distinct time courses of action.
claims.source: A common feature in these cases is that the transmitters have distinct time courses of action.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference from the cited literature on opposing cotransmitters.

claims.claim: Hypothalamic hypocretin-dynorphin neurons synthesize excitatory hypocretin and inhibitory dynorphin.
claims.source: For instance, hypothalamic hypocretin-dynorphin neurons that are critical for sleep and arousal synthesize excitatory hypocretin and inhibitory dynorphin.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about hypothalamic neurons.

claims.claim: When hypocretin and dynorphin are released together repeatedly, the distinct kinetics of their receptors result in an initial outward current, then little current, and then an inward current in the postsynaptic cells.
claims.source: When they are released together repeatedly, the distinct kinetics of their receptors result in an initial outward current, then little current, and then an inward current in the postsynaptic cells (Li and van den Pol, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li and van den Pol, 2006.

claims.claim: Decades of behavioral genetic studies have identified more than one hundred genes underlying olfactory conditioning in Drosophila.
claims.source: Decades of behavioral genetic studies have identified more than one hundred genes underlying olfactory conditioning in Drosophila (Keene and Waddell, 2007; McGuire et al., 2005; Thurmond et al., 2019; Walkinshaw et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Mutant and targeted rescue studies have been used to map the function of many memory-related genes to specific subsets of Kenyon cells.
claims.source: Mutant and targeted rescue studies have been used to map the function of many memory-related genes encoding synaptic or intracellular signaling proteins (for example, rutabaga, DopR1/dumb, DopR2/DAMB, PKA-C1/DC0, Synapsin, Bruchpilot, Orb2 and Rac1) to specific subsets of Kenyon cells (Akalal et al., 2006; Berry et al., 2012; Blum et al., 2009; Gervasi et al., 2010; Han et al., 1996; Kim et al., 2007; Knapek et al., 2011; Krüttner et al., 2015; McGuire et al., 2003; Niewalda et al., 2015; Pavot et al., 2015; Qin et al., 2012; Shuai et al., 2010; Skoulakis et al., 1993; Trannoy et al., 2011; Vanover et al., 2019; Zars et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by numerous citations.

claims.claim: Gycbeta100B has been identified as a 'memory suppressor gene' that enhances memory retention when pan-neuronally knocked down.
claims.source: For example, the Gycbeta100B gene, which encodes a subunit of sGC, has been identified as 'memory suppressor gene' that enhances memory retention when pan-neuronally knocked down (Walkinshaw et al., 2015), but the site of its action was unknown.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Walkinshaw et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Gycbeta100B appears to be broadly dispersed throughout KC axons, based on the observed distribution of a Gycbeta100B-EGFP fusion protein.
claims.source: Gycbeta100B appears to be broadly dispersed throughout KC axons, based on the observed distribution of a Gycbeta100B-EGFP fusion protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Ectopically expressing NOS in PPL1-α3 DANs that do not normally signal with NO is most easily explained if sGC is available for activation in all MB compartments.
claims.source: Our experiments ectopically expressing NOS in PPL1-α3 DANs that do not normally signal with NO is most easily explained if sGC is available for activation in all MB compartments (Figure 4D–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference from the data shown in Figure 4D–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In cultured KCs from cricket brains, cGMP-dependent protein kinase (PKG) mediates NO-induced augmentation of a Ca2+ channel current.
claims.source: In cultured KCs from cricket brains, cGMP-dependent protein kinase (PKG) mediates NO-induced augmentation of a Ca2+ channel current (Kosakai et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kosakai et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The authors failed to detect expression of either of the genes encoding Drosophila PKGs (foraging and Pkg21D) in KCs in their RNA-Seq studies.
claims.source: However, we failed to detect expression of either of the genes encoding Drosophila PKGs (foraging and Pkg21D) in KCs in our RNA-Seq studies (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data in Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: Cyclic nucleotide-gated channels and the cGMP-specific phosphodiesterase Pde9 are expressed in KCs.
claims.source: On the other hand, cyclic nucleotide-gated channels and the cGMP-specific phosphodiesterase Pde9 are expressed in KCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: The activity of sGC is calcium dependent.
claims.source: Biochemical studies have shown that the activity of sGC is calcium dependent and that PKA can enhance the NO-induced activity of sGC by phosphorylating sGC
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by established biochemical knowledge.

claims.claim: PKA can enhance the NO-induced activity of sGC by phosphorylating sGC.
claims.source: Biochemical studies have shown that the activity of sGC is calcium dependent and that PKA can enhance the NO-induced activity of sGC by phosphorylating sGC
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by established biochemical knowledge.

claims.claim: sGC isolated from flies mutant for adenylate cyclase, rutabaga, show lower activity than sGC from wild-type brains.
claims.source: sGC isolated from flies mutant for adenylate cyclase, rutabaga, show lower activity than sGC from wild-type brains (Morton et al., 2005; Shah and Hyde, 1995), suggesting crosstalk between the cAMP and cGMP pathways.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Morton et al., 2005; Shah and Hyde, 1995.

claims.claim: The formation of a strong immediate memory interferes with and shortens the lifetimes of previously formed memories.
claims.source: The formation of a strong immediate memory interferes with and shortens the lifetimes of previously formed memories, and reducing this interference requires a reduction in initial memory strength that can only be overcome through repeated exposure (Amit and Fusi, 1994).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Amit and Fusi, 1994.

claims.claim: Theoretical studies have argued that the tension between memory strength and longevity can be resolved by memory systems that exhibit a heterogeneity of timescales.
claims.source: Theoretical studies have argued that this tension can be resolved by memory systems that exhibit a heterogeneity of timescales, balancing the need for both fast, labile memory and slow consolidation of reliable memories (Fusi et al., 2005; Lahiri and Ganguli, 2013; Benna and Fusi, 2016).

claims.claim: During shock conditioning, multiple DANs respond to the aversive stimulus, including PPL1-γ1pedc, PPL1-γ2α'1, PPL1-α3.

claims.claim: Flies may benefit from the fast and labile memory formed in γ1pedc without suffering the potential disadvantages of shortened memory retention, as long-term memories are formed in parallel in other compartments.

claims.evidence: This claim is an inference from the data and is illustrated in Figure 9B.

results.result: Nitric oxide synthase (NOS) is expressed in a subset of dopaminergic neurons in Drosophila, specifically in PPL1-γ1pedc and PAM-γ5 compartments. RNA-seq identified NOS1 as the most abundantly expressed functional isoform. Immunohistochemistry and expansion microscopy confirmed NOS protein localization in the axonal terminals of these DANs, consistent with NO serving as a cotransmitter.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40 provide converging evidence from RNA-seq (C36), FISH (C38), immunohistochemistry (C39), and expansion microscopy (C40) demonstrating NOS expression and localization in specific DAN terminals. The functional isoform identification (C37) is supported by citation. The localization pattern (C87) supports the cotransmitter hypothesis.

results.result: In dopamine-deficient (TH mutant) flies, optogenetic activation of DANs induces memories with inverted valence compared to wild-type flies. PPL1 cluster activation produces positive-valence memory instead of negative, while PAM cluster activation produces negative instead of positive. This valence inversion is reversible by L-DOPA feeding or cell-type-specific TH rescue.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C33 demonstrate valence inversion in TH mutants with multiple lines of evidence: behavioral data (C25-C26, C30, C32-C33), pharmacological rescue (C28, C31), and genetic rescue (C29, C31). The consistency across different DAN types and rescue conditions strongly supports the phenomenon.

results.result: NOS activity is required for valence-inverted memory formation in TH mutants. L-NNA feeding dose-dependently reduces valence-inverted memory, and this effect is cell-type specific. Ectopic NOS expression in DANs that normally lack it (PPL1-α3, PPL1-γ2α'1) confers the ability to form valence-inverted memories, demonstrating that NO can form associations of opposite valence to dopamine.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C47 provide strong evidence through pharmacological inhibition (C41-C43), RNAi knockdown (C44), and gain-of-function experiments (C45-C46). The cell-type specificity (C43) and ectopic expression results (C45-C46) particularly strengthen the causal link between NOS and valence inversion.

results.result: NO's effects depend on soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) in postsynaptic Kenyon cells. RNA-seq revealed expression of sGC subunits (Gycα99B and Gycβ100B) in KCs, DANs, and MBONs. RNAi knockdown of Gycβ100B in KCs abolished valence-inverted memory in TH mutants without causing general learning defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 provide converging evidence from RNA-seq (C48), protein localization (C50), and functional genetics (C51-C52). The specificity of the effect (C52) and the known NO-sGC interaction (C49) support the mechanistic model. However, the authors acknowledge that other NO targets cannot be excluded (C53).

results.result: NO-dependent memory develops more slowly than dopamine-dependent memory. In wild-type flies, brief (10s) PPL1-γ1pedc activation induces immediate dopamine-dependent memory, unaffected by NOS inhibition. In TH mutants, NO-dependent memory requires longer, repetitive training and develops slowly over 10 minutes, but once formed, persists for over 6 hours.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C63 demonstrate distinct temporal dynamics through systematic behavioral experiments comparing different training protocols and time points. The data clearly show slower induction (C61-C62) but longer persistence (C63) of NO-dependent memory compared to dopamine-dependent memory.

results.result: NO acts antagonistically to dopamine by shortening memory retention. NOS-RNAi expression or L-NNA feeding prolonged memory retention induced by PPL1-γ1pedc activation or odor-shock conditioning. Spaced training with PPL1-γ1pedc induced 1-day memory when NOS signaling was compromised, whereas it normally fails to induce long-lasting memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C64 and C67 provide strong evidence through both genetic (RNAi) and pharmacological (L-NNA) manipulations showing that blocking NO signaling extends memory retention. The consistency across different training paradigms strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: NO facilitates rapid updating of memories. In wild-type flies, a single reversal conditioning trial or DAN activation alone quickly alters odor preference. When NOS is inhibited or in TH mutants, memory updating requires multiple training trials, demonstrating that NO enables flexible, rapid memory modification.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C75 demonstrate through reversal learning and extinction experiments that NO facilitates memory updating. The systematic comparison across wild-type, L-NNA treated, and TH mutant conditions (C69-C71, C73-C75) provides strong evidence for NO's role in memory flexibility.

results.result: A multiplicative model of DA and NO interactions accurately predicts memory dynamics. The model assumes DA induces synaptic depression and NO induces potentiation, with effects following w(t) ∝ (1-D(t))(1+N(t)). This model fits behavioral data for various training protocols and predicts memory decay and reversal learning dynamics, though it cannot account for enhanced persistence after 10x spaced training.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 show the model successfully fits multiple experimental datasets. However, C79 acknowledges a limitation where the model fails to predict long-term memory after extensive training, suggesting additional consolidation mechanisms. The model is well-supported for immediate effects but incomplete for all memory dynamics.

results.result: The interplay of NO and dopamine enables compartment-specific memory specialization. PPL1-γ1pedc (NOS-expressing) induces fast, labile memory, while other compartments (α3, γ2α'1) form slower, more stable memories. Under repeated training, parallel memory formation in multiple compartments allows flies to benefit from fast γ1pedc memory without sacrificing long-term retention.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C118 integrate behavioral data with the compartment-specific expression of NOS to explain how parallel memory systems with different dynamics can coexist. The evidence from different training protocols and compartments supports this functional model, though it remains somewhat inferential.

results.result: Different DAN cell types express distinct cotransmitters. PPL1-γ2α'1 activation produces negative-valence memory in both wild-type and TH mutant backgrounds, suggesting a cotransmitter with the same valence as dopamine. PPL1-α3 and PAM-β'1 do not induce memory in TH mutants, indicating absence of memory-inducing cotransmitters.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 are supported by behavioral data in Figure 2 showing cell-type-specific differences in memory formation in TH mutants. However, the identity of the cotransmitter in PPL1-γ2α'1 remains unknown, making this result descriptive rather than mechanistic.

results.result: NO can act on MBONs and potentially other DANs. Optogenetic stimulation of PPL1-γ1pedc in TH mutants induced prolonged calcium increases in MBON-γ1pedc>α/β (suppressed by L-NNA), but DANs in other compartments did not respond, suggesting limited NO diffusion range (~30 μm).
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 are supported by calcium imaging data. However, the functional significance of NO action on MBONs versus KCs for memory formation remains unclear. The limited diffusion observation (C55) is important but based on negative results.

results.result: NOS is dispensable for timing-dependent valence inversion (relief learning). PPL1-γ1pedc induces positive-valence memory when activated before odor presentation, and this effect does not require NOS, consistent with reports that timing-dependent plasticity involves different dopamine receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 are supported by behavioral data and consistent with recent literature on dopamine receptor-mediated timing effects. This negative result helps define the specific role of NO in memory formation.

results.result: NO-dependent memory requires scribble in Kenyon cells. RNAi knockdown of scribble, a scaffold protein involved in forgetting, impaired NO-dependent memory in TH mutants, suggesting NO regulates memory stability through scribble-dependent pathways.
results.evaluation: Claim C58 is supported by RNAi data in Figure 5D. However, the mechanistic connection between NO signaling and scribble function remains unclear. This result suggests a link to active forgetting pathways but requires further investigation.

results.result: Spaced training with PPL1-α3 induces long-lasting memory that requires at least 3 hours to develop, consistent with reports that protein synthesis in MBON-α3 during this time window is required for long-term memory formation.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 is supported by behavioral data in Figure 9A. The consistency with previous findings on protein synthesis requirements (C81) strengthens the interpretation, though the current study does not directly test the protein synthesis mechanism.

results.result: Background on mushroom body organization and function. The MB consists of ~2000 Kenyon cells with parallel axons innervated by 20 types of DANs and 22 types of MBONs defining compartmental units. These compartments function as parallel units of associative learning with different dynamics. Dopamine signaling plays a key role in all compartments, inducing synaptic depression at KC-MBON synapses.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C24 summarize established knowledge about the Drosophila MB, supported by extensive citations to prior work. These provide essential context but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Background on cotransmission in dopaminergic neurons. Dopaminergic neurons in rodents and Drosophila co-release other neurotransmitters (glutamate, GABA) and neuropeptides. EM studies show co-existence of different vesicle types in Drosophila DAN terminals. Drosophila NOS is Ca2+/calmodulin regulated.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C86 provide relevant background from the literature, supported by appropriate citations. These establish the context for investigating cotransmitters in Drosophila DANs but are not findings of this study.

results.result: Background on dopamine signaling mechanisms in Kenyon cells. During learning, coincident KC activity and dopamine receptor activation increases adenylyl cyclase and PKA activity. In contrast, DAN activation without KC activity engages Dop1R2, Rac1, and Scribble pathways that facilitate memory decay.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 summarize established mechanisms of dopamine signaling in the MB, supported by extensive citations. This background is essential for understanding the study but represents prior knowledge.

results.result: Parallel with vertebrate cerebellum. In the cerebellum, climbing fiber-induced LTD at parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapses can coexist with NO-induced LTP. This balance was suggested to prevent memory saturation and allow reversal of motor learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 draw parallels between the MB and cerebellum based on cited literature. This comparison provides interesting context but is not a finding of the current study.

results.result: Background on opposing cotransmitters. Opposing cotransmitters with distinct time courses are observed widely in neurons. For example, hypothalamic hypocretin-dynorphin neurons release excitatory hypocretin and inhibitory dynorphin with distinct receptor kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C99 provide comparative context from other systems, supported by citations. This background helps interpret the NO-dopamine interaction but is not a novel finding.

results.result: Background on memory genes and subcellular localization. Over 100 genes underlying olfactory conditioning have been identified in Drosophila. Gycβ100B was previously identified as a memory suppressor gene. The current study shows Gycβ100B is broadly distributed in KC axons, and ectopic NOS expression experiments suggest sGC is available in all MB compartments.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C103 provide background, while C104 presents an inference from the ectopic expression data. The broad distribution of sGC (C103) and the inference about compartment-wide availability (C104) are supported but represent relatively minor observations.

results.result: Potential downstream effectors of cGMP in Kenyon cells. In cricket KCs, PKG mediates NO-induced Ca2+ channel augmentation, but the authors did not detect PKG expression in Drosophila KCs. Instead, cyclic nucleotide-gated channels and cGMP-specific phosphodiesterase Pde9 are expressed in KCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C107 identify potential downstream signaling components based on RNA-seq data and comparison with other systems. However, the functional roles of these components remain untested, making this primarily descriptive.

results.result: Potential crosstalk between cAMP and cGMP pathways. Biochemical studies show sGC activity is calcium-dependent and can be enhanced by PKA phosphorylation. sGC from rutabaga mutant flies shows lower activity than wild-type, suggesting pathway crosstalk.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C110 summarize biochemical findings from the literature suggesting potential interactions between dopamine (cAMP) and NO (cGMP) signaling. These provide mechanistic context but are not tested in the current study.

results.result: Theoretical background on memory systems. Memory systems face tension between strength and longevity of memories. Theoretical studies suggest this can be resolved by heterogeneity of timescales, balancing fast, labile memory with slow consolidation.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C112 provide theoretical context from computational neuroscience literature. This framework helps interpret the functional significance of the findings but is not a result of the current study.

results.result: Background on DAN responses and learning rates. During shock conditioning, multiple DANs (PPL1-γ1pedc, PPL1-γ2α'1, PPL1-α3) respond to the aversive stimulus. Optogenetic activation of these DANs individually induces negative-valence memory with distinct learning rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C114 summarize prior findings on DAN activation patterns and learning rates, supported by citations to previous work. This provides context for understanding compartment-specific differences.

results.result: TH mutant flies show weak positive-valence memory after odor-shock conditioning, consistent with previous reports, though the positive-valence memory observed in the current study is much stronger.
results.evaluation: Claim C27 references prior work showing weak positive memory in TH mutants. The current study's observation of stronger positive memory may reflect differences in training protocols or genetic backgrounds, but this is not systematically investigated.

results.result: PPL1-γ1pedc fails to induce long-lasting memory even after 10x spaced training, whereas other PPL1 DANs without significant NOS expression (PPL1-α3, PPL1-γ2α'1/α'2α2) can induce 4-day memory after 10x spaced training.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 cite previous work showing compartment-specific differences in long-term memory formation. This provides important context for understanding the role of NOS but is not a novel finding of the current study.

results.result: Exposure to odors alone did not change existing memory in the reversal learning assay.
results.evaluation: Claim C72 is supported by behavioral data in Figure 7C showing no effect of odor exposure alone. This negative control is important for interpreting the reversal learning results but is a relatively minor observation.
